title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
hook: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
carry: a thread can hold a promise
tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, the night of Shiva, and a hunter who kept it by accident. Your line was stay awake for what matters. Today, a thread.

In August, in office lifts and school corridors across India, you'll notice something on boys' and men's wrists: bright threads, some plain red and gold, some with a big foam flower or a cartoon character on them. Some men have six or seven, up to the elbow. Each one was tied by a sister, or a cousin, or a friend who calls him brother. Ask him to take one off and he'll look at you like you asked him to throw away a letter.
screen: `THREADS ON EVERY WRIST.` → `SOME UP TO THE ELBOW.` → `EACH ONE TIED BY A SISTER.`

segments.voice: Raksha means protection. Bandhan means a tie, a binding. Raksha Bandhan: the tie of protection. The thread itself is the rakhi. The festival falls on the full moon of the month of Shravana, in the monsoon. The ritual is short, and in many Hindu homes it looks like this. The sister prepares a small plate: a lamp, a little red powder, a few grains of rice, sweets, the rakhi. She puts a mark on her brother's forehead, waves the lamp before him, and ties the thread on his right wrist. She feeds him a sweet. He gives her a gift, and a promise: to look after her, to stand by her. A thread costs almost nothing. What makes it heavy is what's tied into it. There are several stories behind it. One, often told, is that Draupadi tore a strip from her sari to bind Krishna's bleeding finger, and Krishna promised to protect her; in that telling, he keeps the promise when she is humiliated at the dice game. The story is widely loved, though the torn sari isn't found in the Mahabharata's text itself; it comes from the telling. In Puranic tradition, a protective thread is tied for the god Indra before a battle; that one is for another day. Today the festival has stretched. Sisters tie rakhis on sisters. Friends tie them on friends. And people send them across oceans in envelopes, so a promise made in one city gets worn on a wrist in another.
screen: `RAKSHA: PROTECTION. BANDHAN: A TIE.` · `A MARK, A LAMP, A THREAD, A SWEET.` · `DRAUPADI'S TORN SARI, AS IT'S TOLD.` · `RAKHIS MAILED ACROSS OCEANS.` · then, large: `A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Rest your left hand lightly around your right wrist, where a rakhi would go, and feel the pulse, or just the warmth. Bring to mind one person you'd protect if you had to, a sibling, a friend, a child, a neighbor, and let the promise form without words.
Rakhi. The thread tied on Raksha Bandhan, the tie of protection: a sister's thread, and a brother's promise to look after her.
Your line: a thread can hold a promise. Tomorrow, the midnight birthday, from the kitchen. Day six hundred seventy-six, done.

howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravana, sisters perform a short aarti for their brothers, mark their foreheads, tie a rakhi on the right wrist and feed them a sweet; brothers give a gift and a promise of protection. Many families now include cousins, friends and sisters tying rakhis on sisters.
